title: Pythagoras' theorem
examples: Teacher, how do I find the longest side if I know the other two?
If I know the longest side and one short side, can I still use the theorem?
Does this only work for triangles on a flat surface?

explain.say: Today we are learning about Pythagoras theorem. This theorem only works for right-angled triangles. A right angle is exactly ninety degrees.
The theorem says that the square of one short side plus the square of the other short side equals the square of the longest side. The longest side is called the hypotenuse.
Let us look at an example. Suppose the two short sides are three units and four units. The hypotenuse will be five units.
Next, we can use this to check if a triangle is right-angled. If a² plus b² equals c², then it is a right-angled triangle. For example, a triangle with sides five, 12, and thirteen is right-angled.

items: If a² + b² = c², then right-angled

explain.say: Finally, we can extend this to three dimensions. If you have a box, you can find the longest diagonal using a similar pattern. It involves three squares added together.

faq.q: What if the triangle is not right-angled?
faq.a: Pythagoras theorem only works for triangles that have one perfect right angle. If it is not right-angled, you cannot use this formula.
asks: Does this only work for 90 degrees?
Can I use this for slanted triangles?

faq.q: Which side is always the hypotenuse?
faq.a: The hypotenuse is always the side opposite the right angle. It is always the longest side in the triangle.
asks: Is the hypotenuse always the longest side?
Where do I find c in the formula?

faq.q: How do I find a short side if I know the hypotenuse?
faq.a: You can still use the formula. You just need to rearrange it to find the missing short side. You subtract the square of the known short side from the square of the hypotenuse.
asks: If I know c and a, how do I find b?
Can I move a² to the other side?

faq.a: The letter c stands for the hypotenuse, which is the longest side of the right-angled triangle. It is always opposite the right angle.
asks: Is c always the longest side?
What does the letter c represent?

faq.q: Does this apply to boxes or cubes?
faq.a: Yes, it can be extended to find diagonals in boxes. You add the squares of the three sides together to find the diagonal squared.
asks: Can I use this for 3D shapes?
How do I find the diagonal of a box?

facts: The theorem relates the three sides of a right-angled triangle.
The two shorter sides are called the legs, and their squares are added together.
The longest side, opposite the right angle, is called the hypotenuse.
In three dimensions, the diagonal squared equals the sum of the squares of the three side lengths.

quiz.why: You correctly added the squares of the two short sides and found the square root of the total to get ten.

wrong.0: This is tempting because you added the squares of the sides but forgot to use the theorem structure.
wrong.2: This is tempting because you added the two sides together first, then squared the result.
wrong.3: This is tempting because you added the squares but forgot to take the square root at the end.

quiz.why: You correctly checked if the sum of the squares of the two smaller sides equals the square of the largest side.

quiz.why: You correctly applied the three-dimensional version of the theorem by adding the squares of all three sides.

wrong.0: This is tempting because you added the side lengths without squaring them first.
wrong.2: This is tempting because you added the three sides together and then took the square root.
wrong.3: This is tempting because you might have only used two sides in the formula.
